Federal Judge Dismisses Trump's $10 Billion Epstein Defamation Suit Against Wall Street Journal

01 Nov 2026, 06:37 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Editorial Desk · Source: www.hollywoodreporter.com

Image: The Associated Press · Source image rights not independently verified · Photo source · Cropped to 16:9; original source image

Ruling Dismisses Lawsuit With Prejudice

A federal judge in Miami has dismissed President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch, ruling that the case cannot be refiled. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles issued the dismissal with prejudice on Saturday, concluding that Trump did not prove the defendants published statements with actual malice, the legal standard required for public figures in defamation cases.

What the Judge Found

According to the ruling, the lawsuit attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting. Judge Gayles wrote that the amended complaint "falls short of pleading actual malice," describing the malice allegations as "conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."

The judge also noted that the Journal's story addressed Trump's denial directly, informing readers that the president decried the letter in question as a fake and denied writing it.

Background of the Dispute

The lawsuit centered on a Wall Street Journal article published last year about a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the newspaper said bore Trump's name and appeared in a 2003 birthday album compiled for Jeffrey Epstein. The source text states the letter was reportedly collected by Ghislaine Maxwell years before Epstein's first arrest in 2006 and his subsequent falling-out with Trump.

The newspaper reported that the letter included text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ended with, 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret.'

Trump denied writing the letter and characterized the article as 'false, malicious, and defamatory.' His lawsuit accused the paper and its reporters of 'knowingly and recklessly' publishing false statements that caused 'overwhelming financial and reputational harm.'

Procedural History

This was not the first dismissal. Judge Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April for failure to argue that the article was published with malicious intent, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint. The president filed that amended complaint in May, leading to Saturday's ruling.

The judge cited the 1964 Supreme Court decision New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which requires public figures to prove that a media outlet knowingly published false information or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.

Key Takeaways

  • The case was dismissed with prejudice and cannot be refiled.
  • The judge applied the actual malice standard from New York Times Co. v. Sullivan.
  • Trump's amended complaint was deemed conclusory and vague on malice.
  • The Journal's story reportedly included Trump's denial of authorship.

Context and Practical Implications

The dismissal is permanent because it was issued with prejudice, meaning the same lawsuit cannot be brought again. The source text describes the ruling as a blow to Trump and his administration, which have pursued adversarial relationships with multiple news organizations. According to the report, Trump is involved in legal matters involving the BBC, The Associated Press, CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, including cases where those outlets are suing for restored White House access after being barred in mid-September.

Trump has frequently denounced media outlets he dislikes as 'fake news' and has insulted individual journalists, according to the source.

Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.

How to Verify

Readers can verify the ruling by consulting the federal court docket in Miami, reviewing Judge Darrin Gayles's written opinion, or checking official court filings related to the case. The original Wall Street Journal article and Trump's amended complaint would also be part of the public record where accessible.

Confirmed information includes the dismissal with prejudice, the judge's reasoning regarding actual malice, and the procedural history of the April dismissal and May amended filing. Reported claims include the contents of the Epstein-era letter, Trump's denial of authorship, and the broader context of the administration's legal disputes with news organizations. Details not independently established in the source text include any internal deliberations beyond the judge's written ruling and any future legal strategy by the parties.
